scope: Chapter13 proof economy and the distinction between scalar, measure and potential limits

edits.old: This chapter proves $L^p$ equations with bounded potentials or prescribed ordinary singularities in semipositive big backgrounds. For arbitrary smooth big backgrounds, both minimal ordinary-type equations follow from strict barriers, resolution and the Gauduchon trace, without either metric volume property. Chapter~\ref{chap:relative-finite-measures} proves general-measure equations in two regimes: the semipositive case under the smaller-background model condition and positive lower volume, without bounded mass; and arbitrary big backgrounds under bounded mass and positive lower volume of the model reference. In the latter regime it also proves unrestricted weighted addition and the ordinary-type $L^p$ refinement. Throughout, uniqueness of the normalization constant is distinguished from uniqueness of the potential.
edits.new:
We first solve $L^p$ equations in semipositive big backgrounds and develop the comparison and compactness arguments used later. These also describe what the positive-exponent approximation selects in the nonuniqueness example. For arbitrary smooth big backgrounds, \cref{sec:big-minimal-comparison,sec:big-minimal-existence} use a strict singular barrier, resolution and the Gauduchon trace to solve both equations in the minimal ordinary singularity type, without either metric volume property. The next step prescribes a general ordinary type in a semipositive background.

For general non-pluripolar measures, existence depends on the background and the reference class. We state the two regimes here and prove them in \cref{chap:relative-finite-measures}: semipositive big backgrounds with a smaller-background model reference and positive lower mass, without bounded mass; and arbitrary big backgrounds with bounded mass and positive lower volume of the model reference. In a Hermitian background, \cref{sec:lower-mass-solvability} explains why a lower-mass hypothesis is necessary for solvability for every measure.

For an individual $L^1$ density, \cref{sec:individual-density-subsolutions,sec:integrable-gauduchon-tests,sec:individual-density-stability} replace this uniform hypothesis by an exact subsolution threshold and its Gauduchon formula. The final sections construct the greatest exponential solution at a positive threshold and separate convergence of the scalar, the right-hand-side measure and the normalized potential. Throughout, uniqueness of the scalar is distinguished from uniqueness of the potential.

The corresponding uniqueness statements in the minimal ordinary type of an arbitrary smooth big background follow from \cref{cor:big-barrier-orders}. That argument uses a strict singular barrier; it does not require semipositivity or bounded mass.

edits.old: Normalization separates the diverging additive constants from the singular potentials. The normalized exponentials converge against every fixed finite non-pluripolar measure. For $L^p$ data the estimate is quantitative.
edits.new:
For solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u_\lambda)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda}\mu$, write
\[
 v_\lambda=u_\lambda-\sup_Xu_\lambda,\qquad
 c_\lambda=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda\sup_Xu_\lambda}.
\]
There are three separate limit questions: whether $c_\lambda$ has a finite limit, whether the measures $c_\lambda\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda}\mu$ converge, and whether a limit of $v_\lambda$ solves the resulting equation. The next lemma passes from the first question to the second for every fixed finite non-pluripolar measure. The third requires a continuity theorem for the Monge--Amp\`ere operator. For $L^p$ densities, the measure estimate is quantitative.

edits.old: The results above solve several Hermitian prescribed-singularity problems already. A research program extending \cite{SGPT} should therefore focus on the remaining identifications and structures, rather than present these existence theorems as conjectures.
edits.new: Ordinary singularity volumes are defined by optimizing mass within a bounded-equivalence class. They are therefore invariants of that class and may be infinite; their finiteness and comparison properties retain the hypotheses of \cref{chap:envelopes}. Multiplier-ideal equivalence is coarser. The $\mathcal I$-goodness problem asks which envelope and volume identities survive under this coarser relation.

edits.old: The extended upper and lower volumes in \cref{chap:envelopes} are invariants of ordinary singularity type by definition; their values may be infinite. Their finiteness and comparison theorems retain the hypotheses stated there. The relative envelope condition and finite damped measures are available without bounded mass. Finiteness and continuity of the undamped measure require their own estimates, which can be imposed on the sequence used in a proof. Multiplier-ideal equivalence is coarser than bounded equivalence and is not built into these definitions. The next comparison with $\mathcal I$-goodness must determine which volume and envelope identities survive that coarser relation.
edits.new: The equation proofs separate three ingredients: relative envelopes, finite damped measures and continuity of the undamped operator. The first two are available without bounded mass. The third requires estimates for the actual approximating sequence, as in \cref{thm:exponential-closedness}.

edits.old: Gauduchon metrics have already supplied an invariant linear trace and the adjoint measure controlling the smooth normalization constant. In \cref{chap:normalization}, the dependence of the scalar on the logarithmic density yields supporting probability measures for prescribed-type equations. Identifying these probabilities with a linearized adjoint at a singular solution requires additional regularity; their existence does not assume such an identification.
edits.new: Gauduchon metrics give an invariant linear trace and the adjoint measure controlling the smooth scalar. In \cref{chap:normalization}, logarithmic variation of the density gives supporting probabilities for prescribed-type equations. Their construction does not identify them with a linearized adjoint at a singular solution; that identification requires additional regularity.

edits.old: For $f\in L^p$, its continuous solution is a subsolution for every $f_k$, so its positive scalar $c$ satisfies $c\leq b_h(f)$. The equations for $u_k$ have uniformly bounded $L^p$ densities, since $c_h(f_k)\leq c_h(f_1)$ and $f_k\leq f$. By \cref{thm:lp-uniform-compactness}, a subsequence converges uniformly. Passing to the equation gives scalar $b_h(f)$ and right side $f$; uniqueness of the scalar gives $b_h(f)=c$.
edits.new: Let $v$ be a continuous solution for $f\in L^p$, with scalar $c>0$. It is a subsolution for $cf\,\mathrm{d}V$, so the maximal-subsolution characterization gives $c\leq b_h(f)$. Conversely, the comparison argument of \cref{lem:bounded-normalizer-subsolution} uses only boundedness of $v$, not of the density: if $u$ were a subsolution for $af\,\mathrm{d}V$ with $a>c$, strict domination would give $v+A\geq u$ for every real $A$, a contradiction. Apply this to the attained threshold subsolution to obtain $b_h(f)\leq c$.

edits.old: The extremal property makes this solution canonical. It does not exclude smaller solutions with other singularities. For $f\in L^p$, $p>1$, it agrees with the continuous solution: that solution gives a bounded lower barrier, and bounded exponential comparison gives uniqueness between the resulting bounded solutions.
edits.new: Every subsolution lies below this solution, so its extremal property is independent of the truncation used to construct it. Smaller solutions with other singularities are not excluded. For $f\in L^p$, $p>1$, the continuous solution gives a bounded lower barrier. The greatest solution is then bounded and agrees with it by bounded exponential comparison.

Under positive lower mass, \cref{cor:positive-lower-mass-exact-threshold} also gives capacity convergence along every $L^1$-convergent normalized subsequence and identifies an exact solution at $b_h(f)$. For $L^p$ data, $p>1$, \cref{prop:symmetric-equation-clusters} gives uniform precompactness. In either case, convergence of the whole normalized family requires identification of all cluster limits.
